subject: Harbor Ledger is deciding whether to shrink live support from 12 hours a day to 6 hours, or keep the current window. The team recommends the shorter window. Reasoning: in a log covering January through August 2026, the quiet half of the day received 8% of tickets, and in a three-week trial in June, when quiet-half tickets were answered at the next window's opening instead, those tickets showed no change in reopen rate or satisfaction score, and answering them at the opening took about two hours a week. In August the two people who both support customers and ship the product logged 11 of their 40 weekly hours on quiet-half coverage, mostly waiting on an open queue that interrupts build work, about the build time the release plan is short of. The plan: publish the new hours two weeks before they start, keep a named on-call for outages, and review the change after 30 days. Prediction, offered at 60% confidence: paid-plan churn stays within one percentage point of the prior quarter. Goal: protect a daily block of uninterrupted build time for the two people who both support customers and ship the product, so the September release stays on the date already promised. Guardrails: outages still get a human within 15 minutes at any hour, and every ticket gets a first reply in the first window that opens after it arrives; the window still runs every day of the week. The team states the trade-off and accepts it: ordinary questions will wait until the next support window, and that slower reply for non-urgent mail is the cost of the goal. The strongest case against: a customer who writes at the new closing time waits overnight, and a few may read that as neglect even when the outage rule still holds.
question: Between a 6-hour support window and the current 12-hour window, which do these facts support, and what would have to be true for the other to be the better call?
why: The slower reply for ordinary mail is a trade-off the write-up names and accepts in order to reach its goal, and the plan still meets the guardrails it states.
